title: Mata Gujri
hook: wife of the ninth Guru, mother of the tenth, grandmother of the Sahibzade, steady to the end

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bibi Viro was married at Jhabal while a battle was fought at Amritsar; your line was joy amid trouble. Today, a woman who was at Bakala too, and whose story ends in winter.

Near the town of Sirhind, in Punjab, there's a gurdwara called Fatehgarh Sahib, and close by stands a place Sikhs call the Thanda Burj, the cold tower. Some visitors stand there a long time, in no hurry. Others bring their children and grandchildren and tell them a story there, the same story a grandmother once told there to her small grandsons, on cold nights.
screen: `FATEHGARH SAHIB, NEAR SIRHIND.` → `THE COLD TOWER.` → `A GRANDMOTHER AND HER GRANDSONS.`

segments.voice: Mata Gujri's life runs through three generations of the Guru's house. She was the wife of Guru Tegh Bahadur, with him in the quiet years at Bakala. She was the mother of Guru Gobind Singh, and grandmother to the Sahibzade, the Guru's sons. She saw her husband leave for Delhi, where, Sikhs remember, he gave his life rather than let others be forced from their faith. She raised her son to lead. Then came the hardest winter. Tradition says that when the Guru's family left Anandpur under attack, they were scattered at a flooded river crossing. Mata Gujri ended up alone with her youngest grandsons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh. A former servant of the household, Gangu, took them in, and then, tradition says, betrayed them to the authorities. They were taken to Sirhind and held in the cold tower. Tradition remembers what she did there. She didn't panic, and she didn't tell the boys to save themselves at any cost. She told them about their grandfather, Guru Tegh Bahadur, and the Gurus before him. She kept them steady. Brought before the governor, the boys refused to give up their faith, and they were put to death. Tradition says Mata Gujri died in the tower soon after. Sikhs also remember who spoke up. Tradition says the Nawab of Malerkotla, a Muslim noble, protested that children should not be punished this way, and a local man, Todar Mal, gave what he had so they could be cremated with honor. Steady to the end, here, isn't the absence of grief. It's a grandmother who stayed herself, and kept her grandsons steady, until the very end.
screen: `WIFE, MOTHER, GRANDMOTHER.` · `SCATTERED AT THE RIVER.` · `SHE KEPT THE BOYS STEADY.` · `THOSE WHO SPOKE UP.` · then, large: `STEADY TO THE END.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a grandmother: your own, someone else's, or an older woman who steadied you when you were young. See her hands and one thing she used to say; if she's living, think of one way to honor her this week, and if she's gone, simply thank her in your mind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Mata Gujri. Wife of Guru Tegh Bahadur, mother of Guru Gobind Singh, grandmother of the Sahibzade, who kept her grandsons steady in the cold tower.
Your line: steady to the end. Through all of it, she stayed herself. Day eight hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Mata Gujri and the younger Sahibzade each winter, especially at Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib near Sirhind, with prayer, kirtan and the retelling of their story.

chat.says: What do Sikhs remember Mata Gujri doing in the cold tower?
options: Keeping her grandsons steady, telling them of Guru Tegh Bahadur and the Gurus before.
Pleading with the governor to spare the boys if they gave up their faith.
Planning their escape over the wall at night, with help from the guards.
chat.meaning: Tradition says she didn't panic or tell the boys to save themselves at any cost; she told them of the Gurus and kept them steady.

notes: The script names the younger Sahibzade and says 'her youngest grandsons'; no counts or ages are given on purpose.
The separation at the Sirsa river, Gangu's betrayal, the cold tower, and Mata Gujri's death in the tower are told as tradition; confirm wording and tone.
The manner of the Sahibzade's execution (tradition: bricked into a wall) is deliberately not described; 'put to death' only.
The Nawab of Malerkotla (Sher Muhammad Khan) and Todar Mal (often told as covering the ground with gold coins) are summarized; confirm.
Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom in Delhi is summarized as Sikhs remember it; confirm the phrasing 'rather than let others be forced from their faith'.
